summary.text: The proposed shift is shown to be a period by a binomial expansion: in the nontrivial case, writing the shift as \(m=n/p\) with \(p\mid m\), every term of \((k+m)^p-k^p\) is divisible by \(n\), using that \(p\mid\binom pi\) for \(0<i<p\). For minimality, translation in \(\mathbb F_q\) first shows that every prime \(q\mid n\) divides any period \(T\), and comparison of the congruences at \(k=0,1\) yields \(v_q(n)\le v_q(p)+v_q(T)\); these bounds imply prime-by-prime that every positive period is divisible by the proposed one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\mathcal P_{p,n}=\left\{T\in\mathbb N: T>0\text{ and }(k+T)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n\text{ for every }k\in\mathbb N\right\}.
\]
For positive \(n\), the number \(a_p(n)\) is the least element of this set. We prove that, for prime \(p\), this least element is
\[
A=\begin{cases}
 n/p,&p^2\mid n,\\
 n,&p^2\nmid n.
\end{cases}
\]
The proof has two parts: first we show that \(A\) is a period, and then we show that \(A\) divides every positive period.

We use the following notation. For a prime \(q\) and a positive integer \(x\), let \(v_q(x)\) be the exponent of \(q\) in the prime factorization of \(x\). Thus
\[
q^r\mid x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\le v_q(x),
\]
and for positive \(x,y\),
\[
v_q(xy)=v_q(x)+v_q(y).
\]
We will also use the standard divisibility criterion: for positive integers \(x,y\), one has \(x\mid y\) if and only if \(v_q(x)\le v_q(y)\) for every prime \(q\).

We begin with two facts about an arbitrary period.

**Lemma 1.** If \(T>0\) is a period modulo \(n\), and a prime \(q\) divides \(n\), then \(q\mid T\).

Indeed, the period congruences modulo \(n\) imply the same congruences modulo \(q\). Work in the field \(\mathbb F_q=\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z\). The hypothesis says
\[
(x+\overline T)^p=x^p
\]
for every \(x\in\mathbb F_q\), where \(\overline T\) denotes the residue class of \(T\). This statement is initially obtained for residue classes represented by natural numbers, and every element of \(\mathbb F_q\) has such a representative.

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(q\nmid T\). Then \(\overline T\ne0\), so multiplication by \(\overline T\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb F_q\). Iterating the displayed translation identity gives
\[
(x+m\overline T)^p=x^p
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(m\). Every element \(y\in\mathbb F_q\) is some multiple \(m\overline T\), because \(\overline T\ne0\). Taking \(x=0\), we obtain
\[
y^p=0^p=0
\]
for every \(y\in\mathbb F_q\). Taking \(y=1\) gives \(1=0\), a contradiction. Hence \(q\mid T\), proving the lemma.

**Lemma 2.** If \(T>0\) is a period modulo the positive integer \(n\), then for every prime \(q\),
\[
v_q(n)\le v_q(p)+v_q(T). \tag{1}
\]

Fix a prime \(q\), and abbreviate
\[
a=v_q(n),\qquad b=v_q(p),\qquad c=v_q(T).
\]
Suppose for contradiction that
\[
a\ge b+c+1. \tag{2}
\]
In particular, \(a\ge1\), so \(q\mid n\). Lemma 1 then gives \(q\mid T\), and therefore
\[
c\ge1. \tag{3}
\]

Apply the period condition first with \(k=0\). Since \(p>0\), this gives
\[
n\mid T^p. \tag{4}
\]
Apply it next with \(k=1\). This gives
\[
n\mid (1+T)^p-1. \tag{5}
\]
By the binomial theorem,
\[
(1+T)^p-1=pT+R+T^p,
\]
where
\[
R=\sum_{j=2}^{p-1}\binom pj T^j.
\]
If \(p=2\), this sum is empty and is interpreted as zero. Subtracting the divisibility in (4) from that in (5), we obtain
\[
n\mid pT+R. \tag{6}
\]

We claim that every summand of \(R\), and hence \(R\) itself, is divisible by \(q^{b+c+1}\). Consider an index \(j\) with \(2\le j\le p-1\). First,
\[
q^b\mid\binom pj. \tag{7}
\]
To see this, note that because \(p\) is prime, \(b=v_q(p)\) is \(1\) if \(q=p\), and \(0\) otherwise. If \(q\ne p\), (7) is trivial. If \(q=p\), the familiar prime-binomial-coefficient property gives
\[
p\mid\binom pj\qquad(1\le j\le p-1).
\]
For completeness, this follows from
\[
j\binom pj=p\binom{p-1}{j-1}:
\]
since \(1\le j<p\), the prime \(p\) does not divide \(j\), and Euclid's lemma yields \(p\mid\binom pj\).

Also, \(q^c\mid T\), so
\[
q^{cj}\mid T^j.
\]
Since \(c\ge1\) and \(j\ge2\),
\[
cj\ge c+1.
\]
Combining this with (7), we see that
\[
q^{b+c+1}\mid \binom pj T^j.
\]
Thus
\[
q^{b+c+1}\mid R. \tag{8}
\]

On the other hand, (2) says that \(q^{b+c+1}\mid n\). By (6), it follows that \(q^{b+c+1}\mid pT+R\). Subtracting (8), we conclude that
\[
q^{b+c+1}\mid pT. \tag{9}
\]
But
\[
v_q(pT)=v_q(p)+v_q(T)=b+c,
\]
so (9) is impossible. This contradiction proves (1).

We now show that the proposed number \(A\) is a period.

If \(p^2\nmid n\), then \(A=n\). For every \(k\), we have \(k+n\equiv k\pmod n\), and raising congruent integers to the \(p\)-th power preserves congruence. Hence
\[
(k+n)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n.
\]
Thus \(n\) is a period.

Suppose now that \(p^2\mid n\), and put
\[
m=n/p.
\]
Then \(n=pm\), and the assumption \(p^2\mid n\) implies \(p\mid m\). We claim that \(m\) is a period. For any \(k\), expand
\[
(k+m)^p-k^p
 =\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\binom pi k^i m^{p-i}. \tag{10}
\]
We show that every term in this sum is divisible by \(n=pm\).

For \(i=0\), the term is \(m^p\). Since \(p\mid m\), the product \(pm\) divides \(m^2\). Also \(p\ge2\), so \(m^2\mid m^p\). Consequently,
\[
pm\mid m^p.
\]

For \(1\le i\le p-1\), primality of \(p\) gives
\[
p\mid\binom pi.
\]
Moreover, \(p-i\ge1\), so
\[
m\mid m^{p-i}.
\]
Therefore \(pm\) divides
\[
\binom pi k^i m^{p-i}.
\]
Every term in (10) is thus divisible by \(pm=n\), and hence
\[
(k+m)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n
\]
for every \(k\). Thus \(m=n/p\) is a period. This proves in both cases that \(A\in\mathcal P_{p,n}\).

It remains to prove minimality. In fact, we prove the stronger statement that \(A\) divides every \(T\in\mathcal P_{p,n}\).

Let \(T>0\) be any period. We compare prime valuations.

First suppose \(p^2\mid n\), so that \(A=n/p\). Since \(p\mid n\), for every prime \(q\),
\[
v_q(A)=v_q(n/p)=v_q(n)-v_q(p).
\]
Lemma 2 gives
\[
v_q(n)\le v_q(p)+v_q(T),
\]
and therefore
\[
v_q(A)=v_q(n)-v_q(p)\le v_q(T).
\]
This holds for every prime \(q\), so the prime-factorization divisibility criterion yields
\[
A=n/p\mid T. \tag{11}
\]

Now suppose \(p^2\nmid n\), so that \(A=n\). Again let \(q\) be any prime. If \(q\ne p\), then \(v_q(p)=0\), and Lemma 2 directly gives
\[
v_q(n)\le v_q(T). \tag{12}
\]
It remains to treat \(q=p\). Since \(p^2\nmid n\),
\[
v_p(n)\le1.
\]
If \(v_p(n)=0\), then certainly \(v_p(n)\le v_p(T)\). If \(v_p(n)=1\), then \(p\mid n\), so Lemma 1 gives \(p\mid T\), and hence
\[
v_p(T)\ge1=v_p(n). \tag{13}
\]
Combining (12) and (13), we have
\[
v_q(n)\le v_q(T)
\]
for every prime \(q\). Therefore
\[
A=n\mid T. \tag{14}
\]

Thus, in either case, every positive period \(T\) is divisible by \(A\). The number \(A\) is positive: this is immediate when \(A=n\), while if \(A=n/p\), then \(p\mid n\) and \(n>0\), so \(n/p>0\). Since a positive multiple of \(A\) is at least \(A\), every element of \(\mathcal P_{p,n}\) is at least \(A\). We already proved that \(A\) itself belongs to \(\mathcal P_{p,n}\). Hence \(A\) is exactly the least positive period.

Consequently, for every prime \(p\) and every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\boxed{
a_p(n)=
\begin{cases}
 n/p,&p^2\mid n,\\
 n,&p^2\nmid n.
\end{cases}}
\]
In particular, for cubes one takes \(p=3\), obtaining period \(n/3\) when \(9\mid n\), and period \(n\) otherwise.
